title: The long view
hookLine: the Buddha's practice took lifetimes, the stories say
tomorrow: why did monks report a friend for saying 'what bliss'?

lines: A NEW YOU BY THE END OF THE MONTH?
SUMEDHA, FACE DOWN IN THE MUD.
HE COULD HAVE FINISHED THAT DAY.
cards: A fitness challenge promises a new you by the end of the month. Buddhist stories run on a different clock.
Long ago, they say, a hermit named Sumedha came to a town where people were fixing the road for a Buddha named Dipankara. One muddy stretch wasn't finished, and the Buddha was already coming.

So Sumedha spread his hermit's cloak over the mud and lay face down in it, so the Buddha could walk across without sinking. Lying there, he saw that he could end his own suffering in that very life. He chose not to.

teach.b: Why not? He wanted to become a Buddha himself, to help others cross too. Dipankara stopped, looked down at him, and foretold it: ages from now, this man will be a Buddha named Gotama.

teach.h: THE PARAMIS, BUILT LIFE BY LIFE.
teach.b: Then, the stories say, came life after life of practice. In the Jataka tales the Buddha-to-be is a monkey, a king, a merchant, a hare, building what Buddhists call the paramis, the perfections, one life at a time.
That's the long view, and it's a real teaching: awakening is grown, not grabbed. But the tradition has a second voice.

teach.h: THE OTHER VOICE: IN THIS VERY LIFE.
teach.b: The Satipatthana Sutta says that someone who practices mindfulness well could see the fruit in this very life: within seven years, it says, even within seven days. So one side says: be patient.
This path is measured in lives, and one bad month is a pebble on a long road.
The other side says: don't hide behind the long road. Practice happens now, and the fruit can come now. The patient voice guards against despair.
The urgent voice guards against drift. And Sumedha's story holds both. He chose a road of many lives, and he started it that very morning, face down in the mud.

how: Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives are told at temples and at home, and Sumedha's vow before Dipankara is remembered as the start of that long road.

o: planning your goals far out into the future
a path measured in lifetimes, walked patiently, step by step
waiting for the next life before starting to practice

games.q: the long road — tap the pairs.
p: lay face down in the mud

s: the stories say the Buddha woke up in one lifetime, starting from scratch
they trace his road back to Sumedha in the mud, and life after life of practice.
Sumedha could have ended his own suffering that very life, and chose not to
he took the long road, to become a Buddha who could help others cross.
the long view means there's no hurry
the Satipatthana Sutta speaks of fruit in this very life. and Sumedha's long road started that morning.

games.q: your cousin says: if awakening takes lifetimes, why practice hard now? what's the best case for the other side?
o: the Satipatthana Sutta says the fruit can come in this very life, even in seven days.
the past-life stories are just stories, so the long road doesn't matter.
a future Buddha will come along and finish the work for you anyway.
games.why: the tradition keeps both voices: the long road guards against despair, the urgent one against drift. Sumedha started his long road the same morning.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something that grew slowly: a tree outside the window, the grain in a wooden table, the lines on your own palm. Nobody hurried it.
Then close your eyes and sit for the two minutes with no score to keep, one breath and then the next, the way a long road gets walked.

wordCard.voice: The long view: a path measured in lives, the stories say, not in streaks. Sumedha began his in the mud.

orig.note: Pali: perfection, the qualities the Buddha-to-be built life by life, the stories say.

carryVoice: Your line: the long view. Patient with the road, and still walking it today. Day seventeen-sixty, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta: fruit within seven years, even seven days)
